title: Lagrangian lower bounds and the dual problem

sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
A constrained minimization asks for the smallest value of an objective on a feasible set. A lower bound on that value can be built without searching the set. Attach a multiplier to each constraint and form the Lagrangian, which is the objective plus the multipliers times the constraint residuals. For a fixed multiplier, minimize the Lagrangian over every decision vector, feasible or not. The resulting number is the dual function at that multiplier.

If an inequality is written as \(g(x) \le 0\) and its multiplier is nonnegative, then at every feasible point the added term is nonpositive. The Lagrangian there sits at or below the objective. Minimizing the Lagrangian can only push the number lower, so the dual function is a lower bound on the primal optimal value. That comparison is weak duality. An equality residual is zero on the feasible set for either sign of its multiplier, so an equality multiplier is left free.

The dual problem maximizes these lower bounds over multipliers that keep the infimum finite. A multiplier that sends the Lagrangian to negative infinity is discarded. The decision vector that attains the infimum need not be feasible.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For inequalities \(g(x) \le 0\) and equalities \(h(x) = 0\),
\[
L(x,\lambda,
u) = f(x) + \lambda^T h(x) + 
u^T g(x),
\]
and the dual function is \(	heta(\lambda,
u) = \inf_x L(x,\lambda,
u)\). Dual feasibility includes \(
u \ge 0\). Weak duality says \(	heta(\lambda,
u) \le p^\star\) whenever the infimum is finite. For the model problem \(\min x^2\) subject to \(x \ge a > 0\), the dual function in the multiplier \(u\) is \(a u - u^2/4\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \(t^2\) subject to \(t \ge 6\). The Lagrangian is \(t^2 + v(6 - t)\). The derivative in \(t\) vanishes at \(t = v/2\), and substitution produces \(6v - v^2/4\).

The cistern lower bound is 11. That is the value at \(v = 2\): \(12 - 1 = 11\). The primal optimum is \(36\), at \(t = 6\), so the gap at this multiplier is \(25\). The decision \(t = 1\) that attains the infimum is not feasible. The bound does not require it to be. A better multiplier is \(v = 12\), where the dual function equals \(36\) and the gap closes.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The usual slip is to evaluate the Lagrangian at a feasible point and call that number the dual function. That evaluation is some value of the Lagrangian, not its infimum. A second slip is to allow a negative multiplier on an inequality written as \(g \le 0\). The added term can then be positive on the feasible set, and the lower-bound argument dies. A third is to treat a finite dual value as a primal solution. The dual value certifies a floor. The primal point, if one is wanted, still has to be checked against the constraints. A fourth is to maximize the Lagrangian in the decision variable. The dual function is an infimum.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Equalities add a multiplier with no sign restriction, and the stationarity condition that sets the derivative of the Lagrangian to zero is the Lagrange rule, provided the constraint gradients are independent. Inequalities add nonnegativity and complementary slackness. Those four requirements together are the KKT system. The same Lagrangian, applied to a linear program in standard form, collapses to another linear program, the dual. Projection onto a half-space is a tiny inequality problem whose multiplier is exactly this construction.
